questions.e: Primes on a die are {2,3,5}, so n(A)=3 out of n(S)=6: P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.q: A card is drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a face card (Jack, Queen, or King)?
questions.e: There are 3 face-card ranks × 4 suits = 12 face cards, so P = 12/52 = 3/13 ≈ 0.2308.

questions.q: What is the correct general addition rule for two events A and B?
questions.e: The general addition rule subtracts the overlap: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), to avoid double-counting outcomes in both A and B.

questions.q: If A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.e: For mutually exclusive events, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)=0.2+0.5=0.7 (no overlap term to subtract).

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number OR a number greater than 4?
questions.e: Even={2,4,6}, greater than 4={5,6}. Their union={2,4,5,6} has 4 outcomes (6 is counted once). P = 4/6 = 2/3.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability it is a King OR a Heart?
In a survey of 100 students, 60 take Math, 45 take Physics, and 25 take both subjects. What is the probability a randomly chosen student takes Math OR Physics?
Two events A and B (with nonzero probabilities) are independent if and only if:
o: A and B are mutually exclusive
questions.e: Independence holds iff P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A) or P(B|A) = P(B).

questions.q: If A and B are mutually exclusive and both have nonzero probability, can they also be independent?
o: Yes, always, since mutual exclusivity and independence describe exactly the same relationship
This cannot be determined without more information about the actual probabilities involved here
Yes, but only if P equals P for both events under the exact given conditions stated
No — mutual exclusivity forces P = 0, but independence would require P = PP > 0, a contradiction
questions.e: If A, B are mutually exclusive, P(A∩B) = 0. If they were also independent, P(A∩B) would have to equal P(A)P(B), which is positive for nonzero probabilities — a contradiction, so mutually exclusive events with nonzero probability can never be independent.

questions.q: A clinic has 20 patients, 5 of whom have hypertension. Two patients are selected in succession without replacement. What is the probability both have hypertension?
questions.e: P=(5/20)(4/19)=20/380=1/19, since only 4 hypertensive patients remain among 19 after the first is chosen.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.25, and A and B are independent. What is P(A ∩ B)?
questions.e: For independent events, P(A∩B)=P(A)·P(B)=0.4×0.25=0.10.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the first die shows a 3 AND the second die shows a 5?
questions.e: The two rolls are independent: P(first=3)=1/6, P(second=5)=1/6, so P(both)=1/6×1/6=1/36.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a 52-card deck, replaced, and a second card is drawn. What is the probability both cards drawn are Aces?
questions.e: With replacement, the draws are independent: P(Ace)=4/52=1/13 each time, so P(both Aces)=(1/13)²=1/169≈0.0059. (Without replacement it would instead be (4/52)(3/51)=1/221.)

questions.q: Two machines operate independently. Machine 1 fails with probability 0.02, and Machine 2 fails with probability 0.03. What is the probability that both machines fail?
questions.e: By independence, P(both fail)=0.02×0.03=0.0006.

questions.q: How is the conditional probability of A given B defined?
questions.e: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), defined only when P(B) > 0 — the probability that A occurs given that B has already occurred.

questions.q: If P(A ∩ B) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A|B)?
Two fair dice are rolled and their sum is known to be 8. Given this, what is the probability that at least one of the dice shows a 5?
questions.e: Sum=8 has 5 equally likely outcomes: (2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2). Of these, 2 outcomes — (3,5) and (5,3) — include a 5. So P = 2/5 = 0.4.

questions.q: In a class of 20 students, 12 passed Math, and 8 of those 12 also passed Physics. What is the probability a student passed Physics, given that they passed Math?
If A₁, A₂, ..., Aₙ form a partition of S, and B is any event on S with P(B) > 0, the Total Probability Rule states:
questions.e: The Total Probability Rule states P(B) = Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)P(B|Aᵢ), summing the contribution of B occurring within each partition block.

questions.q: Why can a test with 95% sensitivity still have a fairly low probability that a positive result truly indicates disease?
o: Because sensitivity and specificity always add up to exactly 1 in every diagnostic test used
Because when disease prevalence is low, false positives from the much larger healthy population can outnumber true positives, pulling P down
Because Bayes' Rule only applies to negative test results, never to positive ones at all, in this context
Because sensitivity has no relationship whatsoever to P in the total probability calculation being used
questions.e: When prevalence is low, even a small false-positive rate applied to the large healthy group produces many false positives, which can rival or exceed the true positives from the smaller diseased group — exactly what the Total Probability Rule/Bayes' Rule denominator captures.

questions.q: For a partition A₁, A₂, ..., Aₙ of sample space S, which condition is NOT required?
o: Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ = ∅ for all i ≠ j
All Aᵢ must have equal probability
questions.e: A partition requires the blocks to be nonempty, mutually exclusive, and collectively exhaustive — it does NOT require them to have equal probabilities.

questions.q: Continuing the hospital infection example (P(I) = 0.26): what is the probability a patient who develops an infection was high-risk?
Using the same screening test (95% sensitivity, 99% specificity, 8% prevalence), what is P(disease | negative test), rounded to three decimals?

A factory has two machines: Machine A produces 60% of items with a 5% defect rate; Machine B produces 40% of items with a 10% defect rate. A randomly chosen item is found defective. What is the probability it came from Machine A?
Using the same factory example (Machine A: 60% of output, 5% defect rate; Machine B: 40% of output, 10% defect rate), what is the probability a defective item came from Machine B?
questions.e: P(defective)=0.03+0.04=0.07 (from the previous question). P(B|defective)=0.04/0.07=4/7≈0.5714.

questions.q: Continuing the urn example: given that the ball drawn is red, what is the probability it came from Urn 2?
What is a permutation?
o: A partition of the sample space
questions.e: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects — it tells us how many possible orderings exist for a given set of objects.

questions.q: How many distinct permutations exist of the three letters A, B, C, taken all together?
questions.e: 3!=3×2×1=6: ABC, BAC, ACB, BCA, CAB, CBA.

questions.q: The 14-letter word SCIENTIFICALLY contains 2 C's, 3 I's, and 2 L's (rest distinct). How many distinct letter arrangements does it have?
How many distinct arrangements are there of all 4 letters of the word MATH (all letters distinct)?
questions.e: With 4 distinct letters taken all together, the count is 4! = 4×3×2×1 = 24.

questions.q: What is the relationship between ⁿCₖ and ⁿPₖ?
o: ⁿCₖ and ⁿPₖ are always equal
questions.e: Since a combination ignores the k! internal orderings of each selected group that a permutation counts separately, ⁿCₖ = ⁿPₖ/k!.

questions.q: How many ways can a committee of 4 be chosen from 9 people (order irrelevant)?
A committee of 4 is chosen at random from 6 men and 5 women (11 total). What is the probability the committee has exactly 2 men and 2 women?
questions.e: Total committees: ¹¹C₄=330. Favourable: ⁶C₂×⁵C₂=15×10=150. So P=150/330=5/11≈0.4545.

questions.q: A lottery requires choosing 6 numbers out of 49, with order not mattering. How many different combinations of 6 numbers are possible?
How many different 5-card hands are possible from a standard 52-card deck?
A committee of 5 is to be chosen from 8 men and 6 women (14 total). In how many ways can this be done if it must have exactly 3 men and 2 women?
questions.e: Choose 3 of the 8 men AND 2 of the 6 women, then multiply: ⁸C₃×⁶C₂=56×15=840.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a discrete random variable?
o: The exact height of a patient in cm
The exact body temperature of a patient
The number of patients in a hospital ward
The exact weight of a newborn baby
questions.e: The number of patients is count data — a discrete random variable. Height, temperature and weight are measured (continuous) data.

questions.q: What must be true of the sample space of a continuous random variable?
o: It must be discrete, never continuous, taking only separate whole values
It must itself be continuous, not discrete, allowing any value within an interval
It must be finite, containing only a limited countable number of values
It must contain exactly two outcomes, like a simple yes-or-no result
questions.e: The sample space of a continuous random variable must be continuous — it cannot be discrete.

questions.q: What does the probability mass function (PMF), p(x), represent for a discrete random variable X?
o: P, the probability that X takes exactly the value x
The number of possible values X can take
questions.e: The PMF p(x) gives the probability that the discrete random variable X takes exactly the value x.

questions.q: How is the cumulative distribution function F(x) defined for a random variable X?
questions.e: The CDF is defined as F(x) = P(X ≤ x), the probability that X takes a value less than or equal to x.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a property of a valid CDF F(x)?
o: F can decrease as x increases
questions.e: A CDF is non-decreasing — it never goes down as x increases, so 'F(x) can decrease' is not a valid property.

questions.q: A discrete random variable X has PMF p(0)=1/4, p(1)=1/8, p(2)=1/2, p(3)=1/8. What is F(2)?
Using the same PMF p(0)=1/4, p(1)=1/8, p(2)=1/2, p(3)=1/8, what is F(1)?
A discrete random variable has PMF p(x) = C(4,x)(0.3)ˣ(0.7)⁴⁻ˣ for x = 0,1,2,3,4. What is P(X = 1)?
A fair six-sided die is rolled, so X is uniform on {1,2,3,4,5,6}. What is Var(X)?
For the same X uniform on {1, 2, ..., 10}, what is Var(X)?
For the same PMF (p(0)=1/4, p(1)=1/8, p(2)=1/2, p(3)=1/8), what is Var(X)?
A discrete random variable X has PMF p(−1)=0.3, p(0)=0.4, p(1)=0.3 (a symmetric error-scoring scheme). What is E(X)?
questions.e: E(X) = (−1)(0.3) + 0(0.4) + 1(0.3) = −0.3 + 0 + 0.3 = 0 — the positive and negative deviations cancel by symmetry.

questions.q: For the same PMF (p(−1)=0.3, p(0)=0.4, p(1)=0.3), what is Var(X)?
A Bernoulli trial has probability of success p = 0.6. What is E(X)?
questions.e: For a Bernoulli distribution, E(X) = μ = p = 0.6 directly — no further calculation is needed for the mean.

questions.q: A Bernoulli trial has probability of success p = 0.1. What is the standard deviation of X?
What defines a Bernoulli trial?
o: A trial with more than two possible mutually exclusive outcomes to record
A sequence of dependent trials whose probability changes as it proceeds
A trial where the probability p changes from one repetition to the next
A single trial resulting in one of two mutually exclusive outcomes, such as success or failure
questions.e: A Bernoulli trial is a single trial with two mutually exclusive outcomes, such as head/tail, yes/no, or dead/alive.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the required conditions for a Bernoulli process?
o: The probability of success p remains constant from one trial to the next
The trials are independent of one another throughout the whole process
Each trial results in exactly success or failure, with no other outcome
The probability of success must increase with each successive trial
questions.e: p must stay constant across trials, not increase — a Bernoulli process requires a fixed p, independent trials, and a binary outcome.

questions.q: Which of the following is a required condition for a Binomial distribution to apply?
o: The trials may be dependent on one another, affecting each other's outcome
The trials are independent and identical, each with the same probability of success p
The probability of success can vary freely from one trial to the next
There must be more than two possible outcomes recorded per trial
questions.e: A Binomial experiment requires independent, identical trials, each with the same probability of success p, and each trial has exactly two outcomes.

questions.q: A Bernoulli distribution is a special case of the Binomial distribution when n equals what value?
questions.e: When n = 1, the Binomial distribution B(1, p) reduces exactly to the Bernoulli distribution.

questions.q: In the same political-party survey (X ~ B(20, 0.25)), what is P(X ≥ 3)?
For the same hospital test-kit inspection (Y ~ B(20, 0.03)), what is P(Y ≤ 2), the probability of not more than 2 defective kits?
A fair coin is tossed 6 times. What is P(exactly 4 heads)?
If X ~ Binomial(n=8, p=0.25), what is the standard deviation of X?
A quality inspector tests n = 15 items, each defective independently with probability p = 0.1. What is P(no item is defective)?
The Multinomial distribution generalises the Binomial distribution to situations where each trial has how many possible outcomes?
o: Exactly one outcome, with no variation possible between repetitions
More than two mutually exclusive outcomes, unlike the two-outcome Binomial case
Exactly two outcomes, mutually exclusive as in a Binomial trial
An outcome whose probability changes with every single trial run
questions.e: The Multinomial distribution generalises the Binomial to trials with more than two (k > 2) mutually exclusive outcomes.

questions.q: In the same hospital laboratory example (n=6, p1=0.70), what is the expected number of defect-free kits, E(y1)?
For the same survey (n=5; p1=0.5 favour), what is Var(y1), the variance of the number who favour?
The Poisson distribution models a discrete random variable that counts what?
o: The number of trials needed until the very first success is finally observed
The number of times a particular event occurs during a fixed interval of time, space, or volume
The proportion of successes observed among a fixed, predetermined sample
The exact time at which a single specific event occurs within a given interval
questions.e: A Poisson experiment counts the number of occurrences of an event during a given unit of time, area, or volume.

questions.q: Which assumption of a Poisson process concerns events in non-overlapping intervals?
o: Proportionality, meaning the probability is proportional to the interval length being considered
Rare events, meaning an infinite number of occurrences within a short interval is impossible
Randomness and independence: occurrence in one interval is random and independent of occurrence in any other interval
Mean equals variance, a property that holds specifically true for the Poisson distribution alone
questions.e: The randomness and independence assumption states that occurrence in any interval is random and independent of occurrence in any other, non-overlapping interval.

questions.q: For a Poisson-distributed random variable X ~ P(μ), how do the mean and variance relate?
o: Mean and variance are equal, both equal to μ
Variance is always greater than the mean
Variance is always half the mean
questions.e: A defining property of the Poisson distribution is that the mean and variance are equal: E(X) = μ = Var(X).

questions.q: Patients arrive at an emergency desk at an average rate of λ = 4 per minute, following a Poisson process. What is P(X = 0), the probability no patient arrives in one minute?
questions.e: P(X=0) = e⁻⁴4⁰/0! = e⁻⁴ ≈ 0.0183, about a 1.8% chance.

questions.q: For the same emergency-desk scenario, what is the average rate λ over a two-minute interval?
questions.e: By the proportionality property, λ scales with interval length: λ = 4 patients/minute × 2 minutes = 8.

questions.q: If X ~ Poisson(μ = 2), what is P(X = 0)?
If X ~ Poisson(μ = 5), what is P(X = 2)?
Under what conditions is the Poisson distribution used to approximate the Binomial distribution?
o: When n is large and p is small, with np = μ held approximately moderate
When n is small and p is close to 0.5 rather than near either extreme
When p = 1 exactly, so every trial results in a guaranteed success
When the trials are dependent rather than independent of one another
questions.e: The Poisson approximation to the Binomial is valid when n is large and p is small, with np held approximately constant at μ.

questions.q: Using the Poisson approximation with μ = 3 from the previous scenario, what is P(X ≥ 1), the probability at least one patient develops the complication?
Using the Poisson approximation with μ = 2 from the typist scenario, what is P(X = 0), the probability of no errors in the document?
What is the defining feature of a continuous random variable, compared to a discrete one?
o: It can take any value within an interval, not just specific separate values
It always has a mean of zero, regardless of the interval considered
It can never take a negative value under any circumstances at all
It can only take whole-number values, never fractions in between
questions.e: A continuous random variable can take any value within an interval (or set of intervals) — waiting times, blood pressure and birth weight are all continuous.

questions.q: For a continuous random variable with density f(x), what must be true of the total area under f(x) over all possible x?
o: It must equal the mean of X, computed from the density function
It must equal 1, since total probability across all outcomes sums to one
It must equal the variance of X, computed from the density function
It must equal 0, since area under a proper density cannot be negative
questions.e: A valid probability density function must have f(x) ≥ 0 everywhere and total area under the curve equal to 1.

questions.q: For a continuous random variable X, what is P(X = 5), assuming 5 is a value X could take?
questions.e: Because probability is measured as area, and a single exact point has zero width, P(X = x) = 0 for any specific value of a continuous variable.

questions.q: Because P(X = x) = 0 for continuous variables, which statement is true?
o: P and P can never be compared
questions.e: Since including or excluding a single boundary point adds zero probability, P(X < x) equals P(X ≤ x) for continuous variables.

questions.q: For X ~ Uniform(a, b), what is the density f(x) for a ≤ x ≤ b?
questions.e: The Uniform density is flat: f(x) = 1/(b − a) for a ≤ x ≤ b, and 0 elsewhere.

questions.q: Which medical scenario is described in the notes as a natural example of a continuous Uniform distribution?
o: Time until a ventilator fails, an example of an Exponential distribution
Patients arriving at a clinic uniformly over a 60-minute period
Number of adverse drug reactions in a trial, a Poisson-type count
Number of patients arriving per hour at an ED, a Poisson-type count
questions.e: Patients arriving uniformly across a fixed 60-minute window is the clinic-arrival example of a continuous Uniform distribution, X ~ Uniform(0, 60).

questions.q: Patients arrive for blood tests uniformly between 8:00 and 9:00 AM, so X ~ Uniform(0, 60) minutes. What is E(X)?
For the same lab example, X ~ Uniform(0, 60) minutes, what is Var(X)?
Time between a patient being called from the waiting room and being seen is Uniform(5, 20) minutes. What is the mean waiting time?
For the waiting-room example, X ~ Uniform(5, 20) minutes, what is Var(X)?
A drug's absorption window is modelled as Uniform(0, 20) minutes. What is P(X > 15)?
X ~ Uniform(a = 0, b = 20). What is Var(X)?
questions.e: Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 = 20²/12 = 400/12 ≈ 33.33 (mean would be (0+20)/2 = 10, which is not asked here).

questions.q: What does the memoryless property of the Exponential distribution state?
o: The mean of X changes depending on elapsed time
questions.e: Memorylessness: the probability of waiting a further amount a, given you've already waited x, equals the probability of waiting a from the very start — P(X > x+a | X > x) = P(X > a).

questions.q: If X ~ Exponential(θ), what is Var(X)?
questions.e: For the Exponential distribution, Var(X) = θ² = 1/λ².

questions.q: The average time between cardiac arrests in an ICU is 48 hours. What is λ, to 4 decimal places?
Survival time after a cancer diagnosis is Exponential with mean θ = 10 months. What is P(X > 10), to 4 decimal places?
For the same distribution (θ = 10 months), what is P(X > 30), to 4 decimal places?
For X ~ Exponential(θ = 10 months), find x such that P(X > x) = 0.05.
A drug concentration Y has MGF M_Y(t) = 4(4 − t)⁻¹. What is the rate parameter λ?
questions.e: Matching M_Y(t) = λ/(λ − t) to 4/(4 − t) gives λ = 4.

questions.q: For the drug-concentration example (λ = 4, Y measured in hours), what is P(Y ≥ 1/4), to 4 decimal places?
questions.e: P(Y ≥ 1/4) = e^(−4×1/4) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.3679, i.e. a 36.8% chance the drug is still therapeutic at 15 minutes.

questions.q: A process has rate λ = 0.5 per hour (θ = 2 hours). Find P(X ≤ 3), to 4 decimal places.
Hospital stay duration is Exponential with mean θ = 4 days. What is Var(X)?
questions.e: Var(X) = θ² = 4² = 16 days².

questions.q: In the Gamma distribution's parameters (α, β), what does β represent?
o: The scale parameter — the average time between events
The population mean directly, without reference to shape or scale
The number of events being waited for, which is actually the role of α
The total probability, which must always sum to exactly one
questions.e: β is the scale parameter, representing the average time between successive events.

questions.q: In the Gamma distribution's parameters (α, β), what does α represent?
o: A probability threshold, unrelated to shape or scale parameters
The shape parameter — the number of events being waited for
The variance directly, rather than a shape or scale parameter
The rate of decay only, which is actually closer to the role of β
questions.e: α is the shape parameter, representing how many events (k) you are waiting for.

questions.q: Average time between chemotherapy side effects is 3 days (β = 3); we wait for the 4th side effect (α = 4). What is E(X)?
questions.e: E(X) = αβ = 4 × 3 = 12 days.

questions.q: For the same chemotherapy example (α = 4, β = 3), what is Var(X)?
questions.e: Var(X) = αβ² = 4 × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36 days².

questions.q: For the same example (Var(X) = 36 days²), what is the standard deviation of the waiting time?
questions.e: SD(X) = √Var(X) = √36 = 6 days.

questions.q: Time until the 3rd post-operative complication is Gamma-distributed with mean 6 weeks and variance 12 weeks². What are α and β?
questions.e: From αβ = 6 and αβ² = 12: β = 12/6 = 2 weeks, and α = 6/β = 6/2 = 3.

questions.q: For the post-operative complication example (α = 3, β = 2), what is P(3rd complication occurs within 8 weeks)?
questions.e: Integrating the Gamma(3, 2) density from 0 to 8 gives P(X ≤ 8) ≈ 0.7619, i.e. about 76.2%.

questions.q: For the same example, what is P(3rd complication takes more than 10 weeks)?
Total radiation exposure follows Gamma(α = 2, β = 5) (β in Gy per treatment, α treatments). What is E(X)?
For the same radiation example (α = 2, β = 5), what is Var(X)?
questions.e: Var(X) = αβ² = 2 × 5² = 2 × 25 = 50 Gy².

o: Knowing one event occurred changes the probability of the other
Knowing one event occurred does not change the probability of the other
The two events can never occur together at the same time
The two events must always occur together at the same time
questions.e: Independence means the occurrence of one event gives no information about the other, so its conditional probability stays exactly the same.

questions.q: A screening test is accurate but the disease it screens for is rare. Which idea is MOST important when interpreting a positive result?

questions.q: You want the probability that a person has a disease given a positive test result. Which concept is mainly required?
questions.e: Reversing a conditional probability, from the probability of a positive test given the disease to the probability of the disease given a positive test, is exactly what Bayes theorem is built for.

questions.q: Mutually exclusive events are events that:
o: Cannot both occur at the same time
Are always independent of each other
Can both occur at the same time
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events share no common outcomes, so if one occurs the other cannot occur at the same time.

questions.q: In survey design, ambiguous wording mainly affects:
questions.e: Ambiguous wording means respondents may interpret a question differently than intended, so the survey stops measuring what it claims to measure, which is a validity problem.

questions.q: Ethical analysis of statistical results requires the results to be:
questions.e: Ethical statistical practice requires that methods and results be reported openly and transparently, not manipulated or concealed.

questions.q: A leading question in a survey mainly threatens:
questions.e: A leading question nudges respondents toward a particular answer, so the responses no longer validly reflect their true opinions.

questions.q: Reporting only the results that support a desired conclusion, while hiding contrary findings, is an example of:
questions.e: Selectively reporting favorable findings while suppressing unfavorable ones is a well known form of reporting bias and a serious ethics violation.

questions.q: A sample selected so that every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen is a:
questions.e: Giving every member of the population an equal chance of selection is the defining property of a simple random sample.

questions.q: Collecting data by observing subjects without any deliberate intervention is called:
questions.e: When researchers only observe and record what naturally happens, without assigning or manipulating any treatment, the design is an observational study.

questions.q: Rounding or cherry-picking data to make results look better than they really are is a violation of:
questions.e: Distorting figures to make results look more favorable than they truly are is a direct breach of statistical ethics, regardless of the sampling method used.

questions.q: Which level of measurement has a true, meaningful zero point?
questions.e: Only the ratio level has a true zero meaning the complete absence of the quantity, which is what allows meaningful ratios to be formed between values.

questions.q: A variable that can only take countable, separate values is:
questions.e: A discrete variable takes distinct, countable values, such as the number of patients, unlike a continuous variable which can take any value in a range.

questions.q: Data collected at a single point in time from many different subjects is described as:
questions.e: A cross-sectional study captures a snapshot of many subjects at one point in time, rather than following the same subjects across multiple time points.

questions.q: In a standard normal distribution, the mean and standard deviation are:
questions.e: The standard normal distribution is defined to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, which is what makes z-scores directly comparable.

questions.q: A z-score tells you:
o: How many standard deviations a value is from the mean
The width of each class interval
questions.e: A z-score standardizes a value by expressing how many standard deviations it lies above or below the mean, regardless of the original units.

questions.q: The mean is strongly affected by outliers.
questions.e: Because the mean uses every value in its calculation, a single extreme value can pull it noticeably in that direction.

questions.q: The mode is unaffected by extreme outliers.
questions.e: The mode only depends on which value occurs most often, so an extreme value that appears just once does not change it at all.

questions.q: The interquartile range ignores extreme values in the tails of a distribution.
questions.e: Since the interquartile range only uses the middle fifty percent of the data, values in the extreme tails have no effect on it.

questions.q: Adding the same constant to every value in a dataset increases the variance.
questions.e: Shifting every value by the same constant moves the whole dataset without changing how spread out the values are relative to each other, so the variance stays the same.

questions.q: Multiplying every value in a dataset by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by the absolute value of k.
questions.e: Scaling every value by k scales every deviation from the mean by the same factor, so the standard deviation scales by the absolute value of k.

questions.q: Which branch of statistics involves summarizing and describing data features?
questions.e: Descriptive statistics summarizes and organizes data without drawing broader conclusions.

questions.q: A numerical characteristic describing an entire population is called a:
questions.e: A parameter describes the population; a statistic describes a sample.

questions.q: Blood type is an example of which level of measurement?
questions.e: Blood type has unordered categories with no numeric meaning, making it nominal.

questions.q: Temperature in Celsius is an example of which measurement scale?
questions.e: Celsius has equal intervals but no true zero (0°C isn't 'no temperature'), making it an interval scale.

questions.q: A variable that can take any value within a range, such as height, is called:
questions.e: Continuous variables can take infinitely many values within an interval.

questions.q: Collecting data from every single member of a population is called a:
questions.e: A census attempts to gather data from the entire population, not a subset.

questions.q: Which type of error arises from the sampling process itself, not from mistakes?
questions.e: Sampling error is the natural difference between a sample statistic and the true population value due to using a subset.

questions.q: Which measurement scale has a true zero point representing absence of the quantity?
questions.e: Ratio scales, like weight or age, have a meaningful zero (zero weight means no weight).

questions.q: A sampling method where every member of the population has an equal chance of selection is:
questions.e: Simple random sampling gives each population member an equal, independent chance of being chosen.

questions.q: Dividing a population into subgroups and sampling from each is called:
questions.e: Stratified sampling ensures representation from each meaningful subgroup (stratum).

questions.q: A study where the researcher actively manipulates a variable to observe its effect is called a(n):
questions.e: Experimental studies involve deliberate manipulation of an independent variable.

questions.q: Bias arising because certain individuals were less likely to respond to a survey is called:
questions.e: Nonresponse bias occurs when respondents differ systematically from those who did not respond.

questions.q: A study design where neither the subject nor the researcher knows the treatment assignment is called:
questions.e: Double-blind designs reduce bias from both subject expectation and researcher influence.

questions.q: Approval from a review board before starting research primarily protects:
questions.e: Institutional review boards ensure ethical treatment and informed consent of research participants.

questions.q: A variable whose effect on the outcome is not measured but could distort results is called a:
questions.e: Confounding variables can create a misleading association between the studied variables.

questions.q: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extreme outliers?

questions.q: The difference between the maximum and minimum values in a data set is the:

questions.q: A distribution with a longer tail on the right side is described as:

questions.q: The interquartile range is calculated as:

questions.q: A graph showing frequency distribution of continuous data using adjacent bars is a:
questions.e: Histograms use adjacent (touching) bars to represent continuous, grouped data.

questions.q: A z-score of -1.5 means a data value is:
questions.e: A z-score expresses how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.

questions.q: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the:
questions.e: The sample space lists every outcome that could possibly occur.

questions.q: Two events that cannot occur at the same time are called:
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so both cannot happen simultaneously.

questions.q: The probability of event A given that event B has occurred is called:
questions.e: Conditional probability, written P(A|B), updates the probability of A based on knowing B occurred.

questions.q: Bayes' theorem is primarily used to:
o: Update a probability estimate given new evidence
Calculate the range of a data set
Find the mean of a distribution
questions.e: Bayes' theorem combines a prior probability with new evidence to produce a posterior probability.

questions.q: An arrangement of objects where order matters is called a:
questions.e: Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections.

questions.q: If P(A) = 0.3, then P(not A) equals:
questions.e: By the complement rule, P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.q: A diagnostic test's ability to correctly identify a true positive is called its:
questions.e: Sensitivity measures the proportion of actual positives correctly identified by the test.

questions.e: Binomial distributions model a fixed number of independent, identical trials with constant p.

The proportion of successes in a sample
The median of a data set

questions.q: For a binomial distribution, the mean is calculated as:
questions.e: The expected value (mean) of a binomial distribution is n multiplied by p.

questions.q: Which distribution models the number of trials needed to achieve the first success?

questions.q: Sampling without replacement from a finite population is best modeled using the:

questions.q: A variable that can only take countable, separate values is:
questions.e: A discrete variable takes distinct, countable values, such as the number of patients, unlike a continuous variable which can take any value in a range.

questions.q: Data collected at a single point in time from many different subjects is described as:
questions.e: A cross-sectional study captures a snapshot of many subjects at one point in time, rather than following the same subjects across multiple time points.

questions.q: In a standard normal distribution, the mean and standard deviation are:
questions.e: The standard normal distribution is defined to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, which is what makes z-scores directly comparable.

questions.e: A z-score standardizes a value by expressing how many standard deviations it lies above or below the mean, regardless of the original units.

questions.q: The mean is strongly affected by outliers.
questions.e: Because the mean uses every value in its calculation, a single extreme value can pull it noticeably in that direction.

questions.q: The mode is unaffected by extreme outliers.
questions.e: The mode only depends on which value occurs most often, so an extreme value that appears just once does not change it at all.

questions.q: The interquartile range ignores extreme values in the tails of a distribution.
questions.e: Since the interquartile range only uses the middle fifty percent of the data, values in the extreme tails have no effect on it.

questions.q: Adding the same constant to every value in a dataset increases the variance.
questions.e: Shifting every value by the same constant moves the whole dataset without changing how spread out the values are relative to each other, so the variance stays the same.

questions.q: Multiplying every value in a dataset by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by the absolute value of k.
questions.e: Scaling every value by k scales every deviation from the mean by the same factor, so the standard deviation scales by the absolute value of k.
